metadata.title: Decoding Contextual Factors Differentiating Adolescents’ High, Average and Low Digital Reading Performance Through Machine-Learning Methods

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PISA 2018 digital reading dataset for 15-year-old students across 38 OECD countries/regions. The manuscript describes data extraction, cleaning (removing cases with >30% missingness), and imputation (school-level imputation within school; student-level nearest-neighbor mean imputation), followed by dummy coding and min/max scaling before training SVM and SVM-RFE models. However, it does not report whether PISA complex survey sampling weights were applied (e.g., student/sampling weights) or whether replicate weights were used. Given the ML pipeline (SVM/SVM-RFE) and the absence of any explicit weight variable or survey-design adjustment, the analysis appears to be conducted without documented complex-survey weighting, which may affect population-representativeness and uncertainty quantification under PISA’s clustered design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the latest-released PISA 2018 reading dataset for OECD countries/regions that participated in the digital reading test (38 countries/regions total). Analytic sample was restricted to 15-year-old students classified into high/average/low digital reading performance using OECD proficiency levels (high: Levels 5–6; low: Levels 1a–1b; average: in between). Preprocessing removed samples with more than 30% missing data; remaining school-level missing data were imputed using information from the same school, and student-level missing data were imputed using nearest-neighbor mean values. Nominal/ordinal variables were converted to dummy variables and interval variables were normalized via min/max scaling prior to model training.

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT use outside school for schoolwork
Teacher guidance on online public info (ST158Q04HA)

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading), 15-year-olds, OECD countries (38 countries/regions)
main_findings.target_variable: High vs low digital reading performance (binary classification using OECD proficiency levels)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (with SVM-RFE feature selection) — HL model: Accuracy (ACC) = 0.957; AUC and other indicators reported as around 0.80 for all three SVM models (exact SEN/Precision/F1 not provided in text). Optimal SVM penalty parameter c = 0.1 for HL model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading) data for 15-year-olds across 38 OECD countries/regions, the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), enjoyment of reading (JOYREAD), reading competence perception, reading difficulty perception, and ICT autonomy perception (AUTICT) to predict high vs low digital reading performance, finding that the high–low (HL) SVM model achieved the highest classification accuracy (ACC = 0.957). This indicates that strengthening students’ socioeconomic and motivational resources alongside autonomy-supportive ICT use may substantially improve the likelihood of reaching high digital reading proficiency, though the study’s cross-sectional design and SHAP-based interpretation do not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading), 15-year-olds, OECD countries (38 countries/regions)
main_findings.target_variable: High vs average digital reading performance (binary classification using OECD proficiency levels)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (with SVM-RFE feature selection) — HA model: Accuracy (ACC) = 0.846; AUC and other indicators reported as around 0.80 for all three SVM models (exact SEN/Precision/F1 not provided in text). Optimal SVM penalty parameter c = 0.01 for HA model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading) data for 15-year-olds across 38 OECD countries/regions, the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), reading emails frequency (ST176Q01IA), teacher qualifications (PROAT5AM), teaching to detect biased info (ST158Q06HA), and reading competence perception to predict high vs average digital reading performance, finding that the high–average (HA) SVM model achieved ACC = 0.846. This indicates that policies and classroom practices that promote higher-quality teaching and more formal, information-rich digital reading activities (e.g., email reading) may help move average readers toward high digital reading proficiency, while SHAP explanations remain predictive rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading), 15-year-olds, OECD countries (38 countries/regions)
main_findings.target_variable: Low vs average digital reading performance (binary classification using OECD proficiency levels)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (with SVM-RFE feature selection) — LA model: Accuracy (ACC) = 0.845; AUC and other indicators reported as around 0.80 for all three SVM models (exact SEN/Precision/F1 not provided in text). Optimal SVM penalty parameter c = 0.1 for LA model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (digital reading) data for 15-year-olds across 38 OECD countries/regions, the study leveraged interest in ICT use (INTICT), ICT use at school (USESCH), online group discussions/forums (ST176Q06IA), searching information online (ST176Q05IA), and classroom disorder climate (DISCLIMA) to predict low vs average digital reading performance, finding that the low–average (LA) SVM model achieved ACC = 0.845. This indicates that improving low performers’ ICT motivation and regulating classroom/school conditions—while guiding productive information-seeking rather than excessive social use—may reduce the risk of remaining at low digital reading proficiency, though the results are based on cross-sectional prediction and SHAP does not imply causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 digital reading for 15-year-olds from 38 OECD countries/regions (total N = 276,269) and builds three SVM-based binary classifiers to distinguish high vs low, high vs average, and low vs average digital reading performance. After cleaning cases with >30% missingness, it imputes remaining missing values (school-level within-school imputation; student-level nearest-neighbor mean imputation), converts categorical variables to dummies, and applies min/max scaling. Plausible values are handled by randomly selecting PV1 in Reading to represent each student’s reading score. Model performance is high across all three pairwise distinctions, with the best accuracy for the high–low model (ACC = 0.957) and slightly lower accuracies for the high–average (ACC = 0.846) and low–average (ACC = 0.845) models; AUC and other indicators are described as around 0.80. SHAP is used for feature attribution and directionality, but the study remains cross-sectional and does not document causal identification or complex-survey weighting, limiting policy claims to predictive associations.
